title: The Nihang dals
hook: blue-clad orders keeping the martial traditions and their own customs

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sevapanthis, service at the center and bread earned by their own hands. Your line was service first. Today, a stream you hear before you see.

Boom. Boom. Boom. You hear it before you see anything: a big kettle drum, struck slow and heavy, carried on horseback or on a cart at the head of a line. Behind it, a tall triangular flag on a pole. Behind the flag, riders and walkers in deep blue, steel at their belts and in their turbans. Year one met the Nihangs at Hola Mohalla, and year three met the elders' army they trace themselves to. Today is the procession itself, and what it's announcing.
screen: `A KETTLE DRUM, SLOW AND HEAVY.` → `A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.`

segments.voice: A dal is an army, a host, a band that moves together. The Nihang dals are the orders of Nihangs, each with its own leader, camps and customs, and each keeping the martial life of the old Khalsa riders. There is more than one, and they don't all do everything the same way. The drum is the nagara, and in a Nihang procession it goes in front. Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum, and that beating it was a way of saying: this is a sovereign people, and it is here. When a Nihang dal moves today, the nagara still goes first. A salok of Bhagat Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the drum a meaning. In paraphrase: the drum beats in the sky of the mind, and the aim is struck. The true hero is the one who fights for deen, who may be cut apart piece by piece and still never leaves the field. Deen is a word some readers render as the faith, and some as the helpless. The drum is inside first; the battle is first a battle of the mind; and the hero stays, whatever it costs. That's what the blue army says it keeps: the outward life of the old riders, horses, weapons, the drum, and the inward reason for it. Some Nihang customs differ from the code you read in the last block. Sikhs hold a range of views about that, and some honor the dals as living memory of the Khalsa's hardest years. This path describes what they keep, and leaves the rest to the panth.
screen: `DAL: AN ARMY, A HOST.` · `THE NAGARA GOES FIRST.` · `KABIR: THE DRUM BEATS IN THE MIND.` · `A HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BLUE ARMY.`

segments.voice: Let your breath fall into the slow beat of the nagara: in, two, three; out, two, three. With each out-breath, picture the drum sounding first inside, in the sky of the mind. Then hold one person who can't easily stand up for themselves steady in mind while the drum keeps time.
The Nihang dals. Blue-clad orders, each with its own leaders, camps and customs, keeping the old martial life, with the nagara drum in front. Today's word.
Your line: the blue army. The drum beats inside first, in the sky of the mind. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Nihang dals process with the nagara drum and the Nishan Sahib flag in front, notably at festivals such as Hola Mohalla, and keep horses, weapons training and their own customs in their camps.

chat.says: Why does that big drum always go first when the Nihangs ride past?
options: It's the nagara. Tradition says the Gurus' drum announced a sovereign people; it still leads.
It's only there to clear the road so the horses aren't spooked by the traffic.
The drum marks a funeral; Nihangs only ride out when someone has died.
chat.meaning: The nagara goes first in a Nihang procession. Tradition says the Gurus' war drum announced a sovereign people, and Kabir's salok sets the drum in the mind.

notes: Kabir's salok 'gagan damaamaa baajio pario neesaanai ghaau... sooraa so pahichaaneeai ju larai deen ke het, purajaa purajaa kat marai kabahoo na chhaadai khet' paraphrased. 'deen' is rendered 'the helpless'; some render it 'faith' or 'religion'. Please confirm Ang 1105 and whether to mention both readings.
'Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum' (the Ranjit Nagara of Guru Gobind Singh) is hedged; please confirm.
Year one (day 280) and year three (days 877–879) covered Nihang dress, Hola Mohalla, the Budha and Taruna Dals and camp life; today focuses on the word dal, the nagara and Kabir's salok.
'Some Nihang customs differ from the code' is stated without naming customs; please confirm the framing is fair.
